questions.question: Q: Rewrite this vague answer: ‘The boys did better than the girls.’

points.text: ‘The boys had a higher median score (68) than the girls (55), a difference of 13 marks, suggesting the boys performed better on average.’

questions.question: Q: A student writes: ‘The data is quite spread out.’ How could this be improved?

points.text: Quote a measure of spread with units: ‘The IQR is 24 marks, meaning the middle 50% of students scored within a 24-mark range, which shows moderate spread.’

questions.question: Q: Compare these two distributions: Town A (median £28 000, IQR £12 000) and Town B (median £32 000, IQR £6 000).

points.text: Town B has a higher median income (£32 000 vs £28 000), so residents earn more on average. However, Town A’s incomes are more spread (IQR £12 000 vs £6 000), indicating greater variation in earnings. Town B’s incomes are more consistent.

questions.question: Q: A student concludes: ‘There is a positive correlation between ice cream sales and temperature, so higher temperatures cause more ice cream sales.’ What is wrong with this statement?

points.text: Correlation does not imply causation. While the variables are positively correlated, causation cannot be confirmed from observational data alone. There may be confounding variables (e.g. holidays, sunshine hours). The correct phrasing is ‘higher temperatures are associated with more ice cream sales’.

questions.question: Q: How should you adapt a statistical report about house prices for (a) an estate agent and (b) a Year 10 class?

points.text: (a) Use professional terminology (median, quartile), reference precise figures, and focus on market trends. (b) Use simpler language (middle value instead of median), explain technical terms, and use visual comparisons like ‘the typical house costs about as much as 8 years of average salary’.
